The chart compares visits to the North, Market, and Harbour libraries in 2019, 2021, and 2024, measured in thousands.

Market was the busiest library at the start, with 70 thousand visits, but it fell at every later point and finished at 36 thousand, the lowest of the three. North moved in the opposite direction, rising from 40 thousand to 55 thousand and then to 62 thousand. Harbour began well behind the others, at 22 thousand, and then climbed, passing Market by 2024 and reaching 58 thousand, only a little below North.

Overall, the two smaller libraries gained readers across the period, while the library that began in the lead lost about half of its visits. By the end, North and Harbour were close, and Market was no longer the main destination.

A ban on private cars in a city centre is usually proposed by people who have to breathe the street, and opposed by people who have to reach it. Both arguments describe something real.

The case for a ban is not only about fumes. Cars take the space that a bus, a delivery bike, or a person walking would use, and they make the pavement feel like the edge of a road rather than a place. If the centre is where shops, clinics, and schools sit, filling it with vehicles that spend most of the day parked is a poor use of that ground. Streets that have already limited cars often become easier to cross and quieter to talk in.

Drivers, though, are not all making the same journey. A parent leaving a night shift, a person who cannot walk far, or a tradesman carrying tools may not have a bus that works. A ban that ignores this simply moves the difficulty onto the people with the least choice. Timed access, cheap parking at the edge, and buses that actually run late would meet the need without handing the centre back to traffic.

I would not ban every private car at every hour. I would keep the centre for people, and let vehicles in only when there is a reason that a bus or a bike cannot serve. The point is not to punish driving. It is to stop driving from being the default use of the most crowded streets.

The diagram shows a five-stage scheme that turns household scraps into soil for street trees.

Residents begin the process by leaving scraps in a bin at the gate. Volunteers then sort that material and take out plastic and meat, which do not belong in the mix. The remaining scraps are combined with dry leaves. This mixture is kept in a bay for eight weeks, and during that time it is turned twice. When the period ends, the finished soil is spread under the street trees.

Overall, the scheme depends on a simple hand-off: residents supply the scraps, volunteers control what goes in and how long it rests, and the trees receive the result. The only waiting stage is the eight weeks in the bay.

Universities are asked to do two jobs that pull at the same budget: teach people a skill a workplace will recognise, and find things out that nobody is yet paying for. I do not think vocational courses should automatically come first.

A stronger vocational offer is easy to justify. Many students are borrowing money and need a route into work that is more precise than a general degree. Nursing, building, and laboratory skills are not lesser uses of a campus. When those courses are thin, people either skip training or buy a poorer version of it somewhere else.

Research is harder to defend in a single sentence because its result is often late. That is also why a university, rather than a company, has to host it. A firm will pay for a study that helps next quarter. It will not reliably pay for a question that might matter in ten years, or for a result that belongs to everyone. If universities drop that work whenever a course needs a new workshop, the only questions left will be the ones with a customer.

I would spend enough on vocational teaching to make those courses real: tools, placements, and tutors who still practise. I would not fund them by emptying research. A university that only trains people for jobs that already exist will be surprised by the jobs that do not exist yet.

Dear Mr Shah,

I am writing about the heater in the living room of 4 Quay Street. It stopped working six days ago. The fan switches on, but the air stays cold, and the thermostat no longer clicks when I turn the dial.

This is now more than an inconvenience. I work at the kitchen table in the evening, and the room is cold enough that I have moved that work into the bedroom. I am also worried about the damp on the window, which has got worse since the heater failed.

Please send someone to repair or replace the heater this week. If a part has to be ordered, I would like a temporary heater in the meantime. I can be at the flat on Thursday afternoon, or I can leave a key with the neighbour in flat 3.

Yours sincerely,
Nora Brennan

A practical skill and a foreign language are useful in different rooms of a life, so I would not rank one above the other for everyone.

A skill such as repairing a bike, cooking for a crowd, or keeping a simple set of accounts changes an ordinary week. You spend less money, you depend less on finding someone else, and you can help a neighbour without making a speech about it. For a person who already lives and works in one language, another certificate in that language may change less than the ability to fix the thing that keeps breaking.

A language does a different kind of work. It lets you deal with a doctor, a landlord, or an employer in the words they actually use, and it lets you read the notice rather than guess at it. Calling that less practical only makes sense if your life never crosses a border, including the border inside a city where more than one language is spoken. Plenty of practical problems begin with a conversation you cannot yet have.

I would choose according to the gap. If someone cannot warm a room or feed themselves, teach the skill. If someone cannot understand the form in front of them, teach the language. Schools have room for both, and treating them as rivals wastes the fact that a person is going to need their hands and their words.
